name: Motion as the actualization of potential
plain_explanation: Aristotle defines motion as 'the fulfilling of what exists potentially' -- so when a dog seizes a bone, the dog is fulfilling its nature by moving, while the bone is treated as simply staying still until seized -- but this picture cannot be squared with the fact that motion is really relative: if A moves relative to B, B equally moves relative to A.
precise_definition: Aristotle's account of motion (kinesis) as the process by which a potentially existing state becomes actual, a definition that presupposes an absolute, non-relative distinction between a moving thing and a thing at rest, incompatible with the principle (basic to later physics) that locomotion can only be described relative to some reference body.
why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as a definition that 'cannot be applied to dead matter' and, for the purposes of scientific physics, cannot be reconciled with treating all motion as strictly relative -- a foundational problem inherited from the whole 'nature as purpose' framework.
historical_origin: Follows directly from the teleological conception of nature.
examples: When a dog seizes a bone, common sense says the dog moves while the bone stays at rest 'until seized,' and that the motion serves a purpose (fulfilling the dog's nature) -- a picture that, Russell notes, cannot be extended to inanimate matter.
objections: Russell: 'no conception of an "end" is useful' for scientific physics, 'nor can any motion, in scientific strictness, be treated as other than relative.'
competing_positions: The relativistic conception of motion basic to post-Galilean and, ultimately, Einsteinian physics.
